content: When you are pregnant, traveling to areas where malaria is prevalent significantly increases the risk of severe complications, including death, for both you and your unborn child. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises continuing other malaria treatments, such as chloroquine, throughout pregnancy until delivery to protect your baby from conditions like hemolytic anemia. After delivery, you may complete your treatment with primaquine. It is not yet known if primaquine passes into breast milk, so your doctor should test your infant for G6PD deficiency before breastfeeding. Drug interactions can alter the effectiveness of your medications or increase the risk of serious side effects. It is essential to maintain a list of all medications and supplements you are taking, including prescription, non-prescription, and herbal products, and share this information with your doctor and pharmacist. In the event of an overdose, if the individual has severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. These tests may also be repeated during treatment. It is important to attend all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose of primaquine, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store primaquine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and do not flush it down the toilet or pour it into a drain unless instructed to do so. Primaquine is used in combination with other medications to prevent and treat malaria caused by mosquito bites in areas where malaria is common. Malaria parasites enter the body through mosquito bites and reside in tissues such as red blood cells or the liver. Primaquine is typically used after other medications, like chloroquine, have eliminated the parasites in red blood cells. Primaquine then targets and kills parasites in other tissues, preventing the recurrence of the infection. Both medications are necessary for a complete cure. The CDC provides updated guidelines and travel recommendations for malaria prevention and treatment worldwide. Take primaquine by mouth as directed by your doctor, usually once daily, with food to prevent stomach upset. Follow your doctor’s instructions carefully. Primaquine is typically taken for two weeks after leaving a malarious area. It is started during the last one to two weeks of your other malaria treatment or immediately after completing it. The dosage depends on the type of infection and your response to treatment. Take this medication regularly and exactly as prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed, and do not stop taking it prematurely, even if you feel better, unless instructed by your doctor. Preventing mosquito bites is crucial. Use insect repellents containing DEET, wear protective clothing, stay in air-conditioned or screened areas, use mosquito nets, and apply insect-killing sprays. Purchase insect repellents before traveling. No drug treatment is entirely effective in preventing malaria, so seek medical attention immediately if you develop symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, or flu-like symptoms, especially while in a malarious area or after completing your prescription. Common side effects of primaquine include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach upset, and abdominal cramps. Remember that your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. If you experience any unusual or severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately. Before taking primaquine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Primaquine may cause dizziness, and consuming alcohol or marijuana can worsen this effect. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Primaquine may cause a condition affecting heart rhythm (QT prolongation). The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low potassium or magnesium levels in the blood may also increase this risk, especially if you are using certain medications (e.g., diuretics) or have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. This medication must not be used during pregnancy, as it may harm an unborn baby. Women of childbearing age should undergo a pregnancy test before starting primaquine. It is essential to prevent pregnancy during and after treatment with primaquine. Both men and women must use reliable birth control methods, such as condoms or birth control pills, during treatment. Men should continue using birth control for at least three months after completing treatment, while women should continue for at least one menstrual cycle. If you become pregnant or suspect you may be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. While pregnant, traveling to malaria-endemic areas poses a significantly higher risk of death and complications for both you and your baby. The CDC recommends continuing other malaria treatments, such as chloroquine, throughout pregnancy to prevent harm to your unborn child, including hemolytic anemia. After delivery, you may complete treatment with primaquine. It is unknown if this drug passes into breast milk, so your doctor should test your infant for G6PD deficiency before breastfeeding.
